title: How I turn ChatGPT's new GIFs into game-ready pixel art effects (full method + free kit)
author: KasperzackGames
selftext:
A pixel effects post here a few weeks ago got a lot of interest but no method you could follow, so here is the full one. The video shows the explosion step by step; the lightning and the volcano in its opening are ChatGPT GIFs (Images 2.6) too, one prompt each, cleaned by the same script and played in a small Godot 4 scene.

1. **Problem: the GIF wobbles and won't line up in a game.** Fix: pin it to one point in the prompt: "The bottom edge of the frame is the ground line, and the explosion hits the ground at the bottom centre, at the same point in every frame."
2. **Problem: chunky pixels.** Fix: "Use fine pixel art: each art pixel is only 2 to 3 image pixels wide." If it still comes back coarse, re-roll.
3. **Problem: you can't cut it out.** Fix: "flat solid pure magenta #FF00FF in every frame". For violet effects like lightning use pure green #00FF00, or the key eats the violet.
4. **Problem: flames cut off at the top of the frame.** Fix: "The tallest flame tips reach about 85 percent of the frame height: always leave empty background above the fire and at both sides, so nothing is ever cut off by the frame edges."
5. **Problem: it isn't real pixel art.** Up to 253 colours in one frame, soft edges, no shared grid. Fix: a cleanup script that keys out the background, puts every frame on one pixel grid, gives all frames one palette (26 colours for the explosion), pins the blast to the ground (frame-to-frame wobble 0.43 -> 0.30 px) and writes a sprite sheet with JSON.
6. **Problem: the effect looks pasted on.** Fix: ask an image AI to repaint the background lit by a fire at the blast point, keep only the pixels that got warmer, and blend that copy in near the blast while it burns. The lightning and the cyan beam get a coded colour light with an ordered dither instead.
7. **Problem: it doesn't feel like a hit.** Fix, in Godot: a 4 to 6 frame hit-stop, 1 or 2 black-and-white impact frames, a 40% flash, screen shake in whole pixels, a few rocks, a scorch mark, embers, and the smoke held for 1.8 s so it drifts away instead of popping.

What ChatGPT doesn't do well: it draws "HD pixel art" (its pixels were 2.5 to 4 image pixels wide, not on one grid), it ignores size requests (I asked for at least 512 x 512 and got 316 x 301; all seven came back with about 93,000 to 96,000 pixels), and results vary. 5 of my 7 GIFs were usable; one was too coarse and one was cut off at the top.

The stick figures, camera, light, background motion and small extras like rocks and sparks are code; the scripts and the Godot scene were written with an AI coding agent (I used Claude Code; Codex does the same job here). The voice in the clip and in the YouTube video is AI.

The full guide and the free kit (prompts, cleanup script, Godot scene, all five effects, MIT) are on GitHub: [https://github.com/kasperzackgames/chatgpt-pixel-effects](https://github.com/kasperzackgames/chatgpt-pixel-effects)

The same video on YouTube, where lightning, fire and an energy beam follow: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zu3a0PBJk\_s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zu3a0PBJk_s)

comments.author: SassyTextDev
comments.body:
Nice!

Have you tried pixellab? They have image to pixel art. It's the "AI image, resize for actual pixels, pick a pallet" step you did in python. But they're doing some additional magic to get cleaner lines and such. Could be good. Honestly, yours looks pretty close to what they pump out, are you really just resizing to fat pixels and scaling down the color pallet?

I always found that "dumb scaling the color pallet" made a dumb pallet. Like... If you generate an image of a bush, and then make it pixel art. The correct pallet is 60% green, 20% black, and 20% other things that contrast well. But if you run it by averaging colors together, you end up with like 14 shades of green, 1 black and 1 random purple (the midpoint between brown sticks and white clouds). There's something *special* about how the human eye sees contrast. Even if most of the actual photo is "shades of green", you only need 8 tops to make a pleasant SNES looking bush.

I started trying to figure this out, and then tried to learn color theory, and decided to just... pay pixellabs :)

Also... I've been playing around with depth masks. They're essentially free on fal. Was thinking. If you did a grayscale depth mask on each frame, you could *bulge* the front parts out a bit.

replies.author: KasperzackGames
replies.body: Thanks. I have not tried PixelLab, so I cannot compare. It is a bit more than resizing: the script finds the grid ChatGPT drew on (or does a content-aware downscale when there is not a clean one), takes each cell's most common color instead of averaging, and picks one palette for all frames in a perceptual color space, with a check that keeps small bright accents like the embers. You are right that it is still statistics, not an artist picking colors for contrast; the explosion ended up at 26 colors, more than an SNES artist would use. Does PixelLab keep one palette across all frames of an animation? The depth mask idea sounds fun, I have not tried that either.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: Why not just utilize the engine's 2d lighting for #6 instead? Split your scene into layers of objects and generate a normal map for each of those layers for your scene instead so you can simply apply light affects at the locations of blasts, that way you're not limited to blasts at the location that you happened to prompt a lit version for.

replies.author: KasperzackGames
replies.body: You are right, for blasts that can happen anywhere in a level, engine lights with normal maps are the better choice; the painted light only works near the spot I prompted. I used it here because the shading is already painted into the background and the relit copy matches that style with almost no work, so it suits a fixed scene. For things that move, like the lightning and the beam, I already use a coded light.

comments.author: m4bwav
comments.body:
Nice, you gave my agent some ideas and we tested them, it had this message:
 
Ran your kit on the example and got the README numbers byte for byte, nice to see a guide that actually reproduces. One idea for when people use several effects in one game: each effect gets its own k-means palette right now, so the explosion and the fire pillar won't quite share colours. An option to map every effect onto one fixed game palette (a .hex or Lospec palette) would make them sit together on screen, and it also answers the "statistics vs artist-picked colours" point above, since you could hand-pick that palette once.
